title: Drugs, Ethnic Profiling, and the American Perception of Colombian Immigrants: A Case Study of Central Falls, Rhode Island.
abstract: In the 1960s, a large community of Colombian immigrants settled in Central Falls, Rhode Island to work at nearby textile mills. By 1985, there were 11’000 Colombians living in Central Falls, where they established a cohesive community. However, that same year after Detectives White and Leganza uncovered a major drug trading operation in the town, Central Falls was branded by the Boston Globe as the “Cocaine Capital” of the Northeast. Following the events, the Colombian community faced isolation and discrimination from other populations in the town. In response, the Colombian community orchestrated an increased number of cultural festivals and displays, in hopes of dispelling the drug trafficking stigmatization. After the Dadeland Mall Massacre in July of 1979, U.S. media has continuously branded Colombians in the U.S. as drug traffickers and “Cocaine Cowboys.” The narrative of involvement in drug trafficking extended to major U.S. cities such as Miami and New York, which saw an increase in drug-related crimes during the 80s and 90s. This research analyzes how the stigmatization resulted in the fragmentation of Colombian communities in the United States. Central Falls, R.I. provides an insightful case study of an immigrant community before and after the War on Drugs. Ultimately, this study illuminates how media portrayals and association with crime placed an additional burden on the Colombian community to create counternarratives that would redeem their image. These counternarratives, which manifested in cultural displays, in turn strengthened the agency and solidarity of the Central Falls community.
